summary: Request timeouts and streaming disconnects for long-context prompts / large max_tokens
description:
Issue summary: Customer reports repeated request timeouts and streaming disconnects when using very long prompts (~30k tokens) combined with large max_tokens settings (>=16k). Impact: multiple production client jobs are failing intermittently, causing job retries and downstream analytics delays.

Environment: production (us-east). Calls primarily go to redwood-7b-32k and redwood-13b-64k variants via the hosted API.

Steps to reproduce:
1) Submit a single request with a 28k-token prompt and max_tokens=16000 using streaming=true.
2) Observe that token generation starts but the stream disconnects at ~12-14k generated tokens and the request ultimately returns a 504/timeout on the client after ~120s.
3) Re-try often succeeds if max_tokens lowered to <=4k or streaming disabled.

Logs/observations:
- SRE logs show inference worker process exceeded kernel time budget and closed connection (worker-level abort) before all tokens emitted.
- Autoscaler did not add new pods for this workload pattern (single long request vs high qps).
- Network proxies show streaming socket closed from the serving-runtime side (RST) rather than client-side.
- We saw a small uptick in memory pressure on specific GPU instance types during reproductions.
investigation_notes:
Initial hypothesis: regression in long-sequence kernel selection + increased KV cache memory growth results in poor tail latency for very long contexts. Alternative hypothesis: streaming flush buffer mis-handling for very large contiguous token sends causes connection resets.

What we tried:
- Reproduced issue in staging using the customer's prompt -> reproduced consistently with redwood-7b-32k and streaming=true.
- Captured worker CPU/GPU utilization and per-step latencies; tail per-step latency increases non-linearly after ~8k generated tokens.
- Verified autoscaler behaviour: policy thresholds are aggressive for CPU/throughput and not tuned for single long-request memory patterns.
- Ran a binary search on runtime kernel selector config: when forcing the older kernel path the tail latency improved but throughput regressed.
- Collected stack traces and core dumps; observed an assertion in the streaming flush code path in one version (runtime v1.4.2) that can lead to a close() call on the stream socket in rare long-run paths.

Evidence links:
- Repro job: logs link: https://observability.redwood.com/logs/job/2026-02-20/ACME-987
- Grafana dashboard (per-step latency): https://grafana.redwood.com/d/long-context/step-latency

Conclusion: two contributing issues: 1) a streaming flush bug in runtime v1.4.2 that can close the stream under sustained long token emission; 2) autoscaler/configuration not adapted to single-request long-memory patterns leading to worker memory pressure on smaller instance types.
resolution:
Short-term workaround applied (2026-02-21):
- Scoped customer to route that pins to runtime v1.4.1 which does not have the streaming flush regression.
- Recommended immediate customer mitigations: set max_tokens <= 4k OR disable streaming; chunk prompts to multiple shorter requests where feasible.

Long-term fix (deployed 2026-02-28):
- Patch merged to runtime that fixes streaming flush handling and avoids premature close() during large continuous sends (PR: github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/2123).
- Autoscaler policy updated to include a memory-pressure signal for single long-request patterns and a new instance flavor (g4dn.xlarge -> g5.2xlarge) rollout for long-context model pools.
- Post-deploy verification: ran customer reproduction job in prod and confirmed stable end-to-end generation to 16k+ tokens with streaming enabled.

Follow-ups/notes for CS/Oncall:
- Recommend customers with frequent very-long-context workloads pin to the long-context model pool or use Dedicated capacity.
- Add a KB article with recommended model/pool selection and prompt-chunking patterns.
- Monitor rollout for 72 hours for regressions (linked incident ticket: INC-2026-02-LONGCTX).
